profile.headline: Senior Data Scientist at Computational Physics, Inc
profile.summary: Detail-oriented and committed engineer with 10 years of experience designing, implementing, testing, and delivering back-end and web applications using variety programming languages and technologies. Specialties in scientific tool development, machine learning, cloud computing, and natural language processing.

positions.title: Senior Data Scientist
positions.description:
• Lead development of Go-based tools, libraries, services, and APIs for a large-scale modernization of mission-critical scientific software used by NASA/USNO
• Own architecture and development of core modules, including O–C Corrections, Calibrations, real-time BDS processing, Partial Derivatives, and Matrix Assembly
• Convert legacy scientific workflows into modular, testable Go components, improving maintainability, documentation, and long-term system sustainability
• Build unit tests and validation workflows to ensure numerical correctness, increase engineering confidence, and support stable production delivery
• Translate complex scientific and mathematical requirements into maintainable software while guiding technical decisions across the project lifecycle
• Act as a bridge between customer scientists, domain experts, and engineers, reducing ambiguity, improving communication, and accelerating delivery

positions.title: Software Developer
positions.description:
•	Develop and build new products and product features for the Mastermind Genomic Search Engine, an artificial intelligence driven search engine used to accelerate genetic variant and biomarker interpretation, clinical diagnostics, drug discovery, and provide immediate insight into millions of full text scientific articles
•	Back-end data processing applications and pipelines handling large amounts of textual, genomic, or similar data using Python and Go
•	Dev Ops and automated testing and CI/CD pipeline using Docker, Semaphore, and Terraform
•	Improve machine learning algorithms for variant search and recommendation systems

positions.title: Scientific Programmer II
positions.description:

•	Provided software engineering support and maintenance for next generation NOAA weather satellite technology
•	Designed, coded, tested, documented, and shipped cloud computing interfaces of high complexity using AWS and Kubernetes
•	Version control and internal code review on Gitlab to ensure quality software development

positions.description:

•	Ensured quality by performing thorough unit testing and team peer review

projects.title: A method for automated classification of Menzerath’s Law in nonhuman vocalizations
projects.description: Menzerath’s law is a linguistic law that states, the larger the size of the construct (e.g., the size of a word in terms of syllable number), the smaller the size of the individual constituent parts (e.g., syllables). Gustison et al (2016) showed for the first time that Menzerath’s law holds in the vocal communication of a nonhuman species. They accomplished this through traditional acoustic analysis, in which features are labelled by hand through spectrogram analysis. While manual classification has been shown to be a reliable means of categorization, it is both time-consuming and error-prone. In this paper, I introduce a method that automates this classification process. Using the statistical program R, I created a mechanism that combines automated feature extraction and unsupervised neural network analysis to search for patterns indicative of Menzerath’s law in raw vocal data. I tested the accuracy of the mechanism by using it to analyze the same dataset as Gustison et al (2016) and compared my results to those published. An inverse relationship between sequence size and call duration as reported by Gustison et al (2016) was found (rs = −0.35, N = 72, P = 0.0009). However, in contrast to the published results, an inverse relationship between sequence size and intercall interval duration was not detected with statistical significance (rs = -0.11, N = 72, P = 0.21). The issues that caused this discrepancy were most likely present in the call preprocessing and feature extraction phases. My results demonstrate that a combination of automated acoustic feature extraction and neural network analysis have the potential to provide a useful new method for identifying universal principles underpinning animal communication systems. I have also demonstrated that R is a viable and accessible platform through which to explore computational tool development.
